title: Indian Seafarers Among Dead as Russian Missile Strikes Grain Ship Off Ukraine's Coast
excerpt: At least five crew members were killed when Russian forces hit a Guinea-Bissau-flagged corn cargo vessel in the Black Sea, with Indian and Syrian sailors among the 17-member international crew.
body:
• At least five crew members were killed when Russian forces struck a Guinea-Bissau-flagged cargo vessel in the Black Sea off Odesa on Sunday
  • The ship carried a crew of 17 sailors from India, Syria, and Ukraine, and was transporting corn when it was hit
  • Eight crew members were rescued from the burning vessel; five remain missing
  • Russia has intensified strikes on Ukrainian deepwater ports that handle much of the country's grain exports, threatening global food security

Indian seafarers were among the victims when Russian forces struck an international cargo vessel in the Black Sea off Ukraine's southern port city of Odesa on Sunday, killing at least five crew members and leaving five others missing.

The Guinea-Bissau-flagged ship had left port loaded with corn and was carrying a crew of 17 sailors from India, Syria, and Ukraine, according to Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi. Eight crew members were rescued from the vessel, which was still burning late on Sunday.

A Reuters witness in Odesa saw smoke billowing from a large vessel off the coast. Moscow has not publicly commented on the strike.

"A civilian ship. An international crew. A route serving global food security. Putin saw another target. This attack leaves no room for illusions. Putin's Russia does not care whom it kills."

— Andrii Sybiha, Ukraine's Acting Foreign Minister

Escalating Attacks on Grain Routes

The strike is the latest in a sharp escalation of Russian attacks on Ukraine's deepwater Black Sea ports — infrastructure that handles much of the country's vital grain and cargo exports. Over the past several weeks, Russia has systematically targeted port facilities, commercial vessels, and maritime infrastructure in what analysts describe as a deliberate campaign to cripple Ukraine's wartime economy.

On Saturday, one person was killed when Russia attacked port infrastructure in Odesa, hitting a vessel flying the flag of Antigua and Barbuda. A day earlier, three more people were killed in Russian strikes on Odesa and Mykolaiv.

Ukraine's seaports authority reported that Russian attacks on ports and civilian vessels killed 11 people in July alone, including port workers and foreign crew members. The strikes have led to a partial halt in grain shipments and an almost complete suspension of grain purchases at port terminals, according to traders and analysts.

Impact on Global Food Supply

Ukraine, one of the world's largest grain exporters, shipped more than 37 million metric tons of grain last season through its Black Sea ports. The country's main farmers' union estimates it has lost roughly a third of its port export capacity due to the intensifying attacks.

The disruption has already driven wheat prices higher on global markets. Four of Ukraine's 13 large grain export terminals have suspended purchases, and some shipowners are refusing to enter Ukrainian ports out of fear of further strikes.

Deputy Economy Minister Taras Vysotskiy told Reuters the state would "do everything possible to preserve minimum guaranteed export volumes to support international food security."

Indian Seafarers in the Line of Fire

India is one of the world's largest suppliers of merchant seafarers, with an estimated 240,000 Indian nationals serving on commercial vessels globally. The attack highlights the growing risks faced by civilian mariners navigating trade routes through active conflict zones.

This is not the first time Indian crew members have been caught in the Russia-Ukraine crossfire at sea. As both sides escalate maritime attacks — Ukraine claims to have struck 147 Russian vessels this month alone — the Black Sea has become one of the most dangerous waterways for civilian shipping since the Second World War.
